evidence: Mart. 13.52.2: pectore tantum et cervīce sapit
Cato Agr. 66.1 (Lewis & Short s.v. sapiō): oleum male sapiet
terms.comment: No ancient interjection for relishing food is known. Sapere with an adverb is the classical way to say how a thing tastes.

evidence: Hor. S. 2.8.92, of dishes (Lewis & Short s.v. suāvis)
Varr. ap. Non. 81 (Lewis & Short s.v. pāpa)
terms.comment: Varro reports that small children call their food pappa, their mother mamma and their father tata.

evidence: Plaut. Epid. 5.2.62, in Lewis & Short’s numbering; Pers. 3.17

phrases.latin: tōta quidem pōnātur anas, sed pectore tantum et cervīce sapit
phrases.english: by all means serve the whole duck, but only the breast and neck taste good

pappa.against: Lewis & Short pāpa, with pappa as a variant
pappa.html: The spelling of the verb pappō (Lewis & Short; Pers. 3.17) and of Varro’s fragment in the Latinitas loci text (pappās, Non. p. 81): the heavy first syllable is written with the double consonant, as in mamma. Cf. Italian pappa, baby food.

sources: Lewis & Short: sapio · Lewis & Short: suavis · Lewis & Short: papa · Lewis & Short: pappo
Martial from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-martialis); Varro’s report also in loci-varro.
